messages.content: A tool fails with 'error: lock held by another process'. Write the documentation entry a user finds when they search that string: what it means, the two situations that cause it, and what to do in each. Around 200 words.

## error: lock held by another process

Before it writes anything, the tool takes an exclusive lock. That keeps two copies from interleaving their writes and leaving you with state that's half one run and half the other. This message means the lock was already taken when it asked for it.

There are two reasons for that.

Usually another run genuinely is going. A second terminal, an editor plugin, a git hook, a CI job pointed at the same checkout. Nothing is broken here — the lock is doing the job it exists for. Most runs finish quickly, so wait and try again. To see who's holding it, `lsof <lockfile>` on Linux or macOS will name the process, and so will `fuser -v <lockfile>`.

The other reason is a stale lock. An earlier run took a SIGKILL, or lost power, or sat inside a container that got yanked out from under it, and the lock file outlived the process. You'll know because `lsof` reports nobody. That is the one case where you remove the lock file by hand and run again.

Look before you delete. Removing a live lock doesn't stop whoever owns it. It just lets a second run start alongside the first, which is the corruption the lock was there to prevent.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
## error: lock held by another process

The tool grabs an exclusive lock before it writes a single byte. That stops two copies from interleaving their writes and leaving you with state that's half one run and half another. This message means something already held the lock when the tool asked for it.

Two things cause that.

Nine times out of ten a second run really is in progress. Another terminal, an editor plugin, a git hook, a CI job pointed at the same checkout. Nothing has gone wrong; the lock is doing the job it exists to do. Runs are usually short, so wait a moment and try again. To find out who holds it, `lsof <lockfile>` names the process on Linux and macOS, and `fuser -v <lockfile>` will too.

The other cause is a stale lock. An earlier run caught a SIGKILL, or the power went, or its container was pulled out from under it, and the lock file outlived the process that made it. The tell is `lsof` coming back empty. That is the one case where you delete the lock file by hand and run again.

Check before you delete. Removing a live lock doesn't stop its owner. It only lets a second run start alongside the first, which is the corruption the lock was there to prevent.
